The conclusion (PDF p.14) instead states total sorption capacity of 178.11 mg/g. The table total is internally consistent: 97.12 + 61.85 + 28.14 = 187.11 mg/g, and 9.36 mg / 0.050 g = 187.2 mg/g (rounding). The conclusion is 9.00 mg/g lower and does not match the table or qtotal/mass calculation. This is a conclusion-text arithmetic/transcription error, not a reason to replace the table value. The third-cycle capacity is only 28.14 mg/g, showing substantial decline. Table 6 uses 20 mg/L CIP, 1.5 mL/min, 50 mg AAB; cycle 2 and 3 qbed are 61.85 and 28.14 mg/g.
Why it matters: The review must not quote both totals as if consistent. The correct table-supported cumulative value is 187.11 mg/g, with transparent arithmetic; the 178.11 mg/g conclusion figure is an apparent typo. The cycle-wise fall from 97.12 to 28.14 mg/g is material for practical regeneration claims.
Next action: Use Table 6 total 187.11 mg/g and independently state arithmetic (9.36 mg total adsorbed / 0.050 g initial bed = 187.2 mg/g, rounding). Flag conclusion's 178.11 as a source typo. Preserve cycle-wise qbed decay and avoid claiming high regeneration stability.
Resolution route: Original full PDF rendered and visually inspected; table arithmetic independently checked.
Manuscript treatment until resolved: Report three-cycle total from Table 6 as 187.11 mg/g (qbed sum); note conclusion text gives inconsistent 178.11 mg/g and is not used. Highlight qbed decline 97.12→61.85→28.14 mg/g.
Status: Resolved for manuscript use — Table 6 total internally consistent; conclusion typo flagged
Primary-source verification: Verified against original full Springer PDF, rendered Table 6 and conclusion.

Paper: Liu et al. (2025), kaolin–alginate beads for chlortetracycline
Specific unresolved issue: Original Royal Society Open Science PDF §3.5 (PDF pp.14–15) defines adsorption cost as adsorbent cost (US$/g adsorbent) divided by adsorption capacity (mg/g) ×10−3, yielding US$/g CTC. It lists sodium alginate at US$8.36/kg, kaolin at US$3.90/kg and CaCl2 at US$10.59/kg, but states the electricity price as 0.0175 US$ g−1. That is dimensionally a price per gram of electricity rather than a conventional electricity tariff (e.g. US$/kWh); no energy quantity, equipment power/runtime, bead yield or full bill of materials is shown in this section to reconstruct it. Assuming four cycles, authors report CTC removal cost 0.095 US$/g for KN@Alg and 0.15 US$/g for activated carbon. The cost basis includes chemical and energy inputs only; it does not transparently include labour, water, equipment/capital, bead yield, pumping, column support, eluent/chemical regeneration, spent regeneration stream or end-of-life. The four-cycle assumption is a short lab reuse test, and regeneration curves are not stable across eluents. Practical tests use 5 mg/L spiked distilled/tap/river water; column maintains 93.6% removal over 20 bed volumes, not proof of native trace-level wastewater performance.
Why it matters: The reported electricity unit is dimensionally anomalous and the energy calculation cannot be independently reproduced from the presented data. The apparent 0.095 vs 0.15 US$/g advantage is a narrow laboratory material/energy estimate, not a full process cost or lifecycle advantage; the four-cycle assumption and regeneration effluent are material boundary conditions.
Next action: Retain the two reported unit costs as author-calculated estimates only. Do not reinterpret 0.0175 US$/g as US$/kWh without author confirmation. Request the energy tariff unit, kWh consumed per batch/kg beads, product yield and cost worksheet only if cost ranking is central. Include four-cycle assumption and regeneration effluent in limitations.
Resolution route: Original full Royal Society Open Science PDF visually checked; no supplementary cost worksheet found in current Library search.
Manuscript treatment until resolved: State authors estimate 0.095 US$/g CTC for KN@Alg versus 0.15 US$/g for AC assuming four reuse cycles, but the stated electricity price unit (US$/g) is dimensionally anomalous and the calculation lacks transparent energy/yield and downstream process boundaries. Do not call this a validated TEA/LCA or general cost advantage.
Status: Open — anomalous electricity unit and incomplete process-cost boundary confirmed
Primary-source verification: Verified against original Royal Society Open Science full PDF and rendered cost/column/regeneration pages.
Source pinpoints visually checked: PDF pp.14–15 §3.5 and Eq.3.1 (electricity unit and cost formula); PDF p.15 Fig.10 (spiked-water cartridge/column); PDF p.14 Fig.9 and §3.3 (regeneration).
